content.text: PR #176 now follows the template. On to step 2, restructuring the issues. I'll write the ten sub-issues of the epic from the agreed plan, each with why, what to do, and done-when:

input.content:
[
 {"key":"spike","title":"Spike: test the sandbox assumptions on a Mac before RFC-0011","labels":["security","testing","P1"],"body":"## Why

The sandbox plan in #141 rests on three assumptions no one has tested. RFC-0011 and the setup skill should be written against what is true, not what is assumed.

## What to do

- [ ] With a throwaway Claude Code profile on macOS, turn on `sandbox.enabled`, `failIfUnavailable` and `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`.
- [ ] **Keychain.** Check whether a sandboxed Bash command can read gh's token and git's osxkeychain credential from the macOS keychain (for example `gh auth token`, or `git credential fill` for github.com).
- [ ] **Hooks.** Check that the plugin's hooks run outside the sandbox: from a hook, read a file that the sandbox denies to Bash.
- [ ] **MCP server.** Check that a plugin-bundled MCP server runs outside the sandbox, with the user's normal gh login, and that a PreToolUse hook matches its tool names.
- [ ] **Edit deny rules.** Check whether `Edit` deny rules for the layer's records also stop sandboxed Bash from writing them, and whether a symbolic link inside the project to a denied path is denied too.
- [ ] Record each result, with the exact settings and commands used, as a comment on #141.

## Done when

- Each assumption has a recorded yes or no, and #141's design is adjusted where an answer is no.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"rfc","title":"RFC-0011: a declared OS boundary as the condition for relaxing a shell call","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

Standard 1.2.0 §5.18.3 lets a layer classify a call from its arguments and relax it below the tool's worst case. For a shell, that classification reads text, which cannot be made sound (#141). Standard 1.2.0 is still a Candidate, so this can be fixed before it is released.

## What to do

- [ ] Write `spec/RFC-0011-*.md` with the sections `spec/GOVERNANCE.md` requires (motivation, alternatives, backward compatibility, conformance tests), marked as amending Standard 1.2.0.
- [ ] §10.4: a conformance statement names, for each shell-like tool, the operating-system boundary its calls run under, or "none".
- [ ] §5.18.3: a classifier may relax a call of such a tool below the tool's worst case only when a boundary is declared. A layer without one stays conformant, with every call of the tool at its worst case.
- [ ] Define what a boundary must hold for this purpose: writes limited to the scope, no write to the layer's records, a network allowlist, and the layer's own credentials out of reach.
- [ ] Update the statement schema (`tests/conformance/calls/schema/statement.schema.json`), both reference statements, `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` and the CHANGELOG.
- [ ] Use the spike's findings.

## Done when

- RFC-0011 is Accepted and Standard 1.2.0 carries the rule.
- `python tools/validate_rfcs.py` passes, and both statements declare their boundary.

## Related

- #141, #137 (the release waits for this)"},
 {"key":"setup","title":"Add a setup skill that writes the sandbox settings","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

A plugin cannot change a user's settings on its own. Without the sandbox settings, every Bash call stays gated under RFC-0011, so users need a guided way to turn the sandbox on.

## What to do

- [ ] Add a skill (`/grounded-setup`) that shows the settings it will write as a diff, asks, then writes them to user scope (`~/.claude/settings.json`):
  - `sandbox.enabled: true`, `failIfUnavailable: true`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, and no `excludedCommands`;
  - `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` (see the network allowlist sub-issue);
  - Edit and Read deny rules for the layer's records (see the deny-rules sub-issue);
  - credential deny entries for the audit key file and for the usual token files and variables: `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.ssh`, `GH_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
- [ ] Leave every other setting alone, and keep the skill safe to run again.
- [ ] On a platform with no sandbox (native Windows), say so and write nothing.
- [ ] Document it in `hooks/README.md` and the README.

## Done when

- On a fresh macOS and Linux profile, running the skill and accepting gives settings under which the relax rule applies and the boundary tests pass.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"relax","title":"Relax read-only Bash only under a verified strict sandbox (plugin hook)","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

Under RFC-0011, the pre-tool-use hook may let a read-only Bash command skip the checkpoint and approval only when an operating-system boundary holds.

## What to do

- [ ] In `hooks/pretooluse_require_checkpoint.sh`, read the effective `sandbox` settings from user and managed settings only, never from the project's, which a repository controls.
- [ ] Relax read-only Bash only when `enabled`, `failIfUnavailable` and `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` all hold. Otherwise classify every Bash call as a gated `mutate`.
- [ ] Treat a Bash call that sets `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` as a gated `mutate`.
- [ ] Say in the refusal text how to enable the sandbox (the setup skill).
- [ ] Tests: a sandbox off, missing, or partly configured in each scope; project settings that try to claim a sandbox.

## Done when

- With the strict sandbox, read-only commands pass as today. Without it, every Bash call needs a checkpoint and approval. Project settings cannot change which applies.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"deny","title":"Protect the layer's records with deny rules, not the records guard","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

The records guard decides from command text whether a call writes the layer's records (`.claude/checkpoint.ok`, `.claude/checkpoints/`, `.claude/audit.log` and its head, `<git dir>/acs/`). Many security-loop findings were routes past it. Edit deny rules are enforced by the sandbox for Bash, and by the permission system for the file tools.

## What to do

- [ ] Define Edit and Read deny rules for those paths, as the setup skill writes them.
- [ ] Check how the rules handle `<git dir>` (a worktree, a `.git` file) and symbolic links. Use the spike's findings.
- [ ] Document the records guard as an advisory early refusal (`hooks/README.md`, SECURITY.md §5.5).
- [ ] Boundary tests: write each record from Bash and from Edit or Write, through several spellings and a link, and expect each attempt to fail.

## Done when

- Under the setup skill's settings, no Bash command or file tool writes a record, whatever its spelling.

## Related

- #141, #143"},
 {"key":"network","title":"Fill the sandbox's network allowlist from the domain profile","labels":["enhancement","security","P2"],"body":"## Why

The send skill hook decides from command text whether a request goes to a private address or an unlisted host. A network allowlist enforced by the sandbox holds whatever the spelling. The Standard already has a destination policy (`allowed_destinations` in a domain profile).

## What to do

- [ ] In the setup skill, build `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` from the active domain profile's `allowed_destinations`, plus the package registries the project uses (detected from its manifests).
- [ ] Say what happens when no profile is active: a minimal list, shown to the user before writing.
- [ ] Document the send hook as advisory.
- [ ] Boundary tests: reach an unlisted host, a private address and the cloud metadata address from Bash, through several spellings, and expect each to fail.

## Done when

- Under the setup skill's settings, Bash reaches only the listed hosts.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"key","title":"Keep the audit log's HMAC key in a file out of the agent's reach","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

The log hook signs the audit log with `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY`. When that is unset, it derives the key from the hostname, which any process can recompute. The agent's own commands can also read the variable, so a cut log can be signed again.

## What to do

- [ ] The setup skill generates a random key into `~/.config/acs/audit.key` (mode 600).
- [ ] The hooks, which run outside the sandbox, read it. The setup skill adds a sandbox credential deny entry and Read deny rules for it.
- [ ] Remove the hostname-derived fallback. Without a key, lines are logged unsigned and the hook says so (exit 1).
- [ ] Keep `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` working where it is set, for compatibility, and say in the docs that the file is preferred.
- [ ] Update `tools/verify_audit_log.py`, SECURITY.md, `hooks/README.md` and the CHANGELOG (an upgrade note).
- [ ] Boundary test: read the key from Bash and from Read, and expect both to fail.

## Done when

- Under the setup skill's settings, nothing the agent runs can read the key, and no key is derived from the hostname.

## Related

- #141, #143"},
 {"key":"adapter","title":"Turn on a strict sandbox by default in the Python adapter","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

`GroundedAgentAdapter.wrap_options` builds the Agent SDK options itself, so it can turn the sandbox on directly (`ClaudeAgentOptions.sandbox`).

## What to do

- [ ] By default, `wrap_options` sets a strict sandbox (`enabled`, no unsandboxed escape, `failIfUnavailable` where the SDK supports it) and the deny rules for the layer's records. A caller who passes its own `sandbox` settings keeps them.
- [ ] The Bash classifier relaxes read-only commands only when the resulting options hold that strict sandbox. Otherwise every Bash call is a gated `mutate`.
- [ ] The adapter's conformance statement declares the boundary (RFC-0011).

- A default-wrapped session runs Bash sandboxed, and read-only commands are relaxed only then.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"broker","title":"Add typed remote-write tools and deny git and gh credentials to Bash","labels":["enhancement","security","P2"],"body":"## Why

A sandbox does not stop an authorised destructive remote write (a force push, a merge, a release) while the credential is in reach. Typed tools carry the facts an approval needs as fields, not as shell text.

## What to do

- [ ] Ship an MCP server with the plugin with tools bound under §5.18.1: `push` (branch, `force_with_lease`), `tag_push`, `pr_create`, `pr_merge` (number, method), `release_create`, `issue_create` and `issue_assign`. Each is a gated `mutate` or `send`, with its checkpoint and approval.

  - runs no shell: git and gh are started by argument list, with `core.hooksPath` pointed at nothing;
  - takes one action per call, so an approval covers one PR or tag.
- [ ] The setup skill denies git and gh credentials to Bash (use the spike's keychain findings).
- [ ] Boundary tests: push, merge and release from Bash through several spellings, and expect each to fail; a typed merge asks once for one PR.

- Under the setup skill's settings, remote writes happen only through the typed tools, each approved for its own target.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"tests","title":"Add boundary tests that attack the sandbox in CI (macOS and Linux)","labels":["testing","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

The current hook tests check how command text is read. The new design needs tests that attack the boundary itself and pass only if every route fails, however it is spelled.

## What to do

- [ ] A test suite that runs commands under Claude Code's sandbox with the setup skill's settings, on macOS (Seatbelt) and Linux (bubblewrap) CI jobs.
- [ ] Routes, each through several spellings (substitution, `env`, an absolute path, a script, an interpreter, `find -exec`, a link):
  - write each of the layer's records;
  - read the audit key and a token file;
  - reach an unlisted host;
  - push, merge or release without the typed tools;
  - write outside the project.
- [ ] A control in which each route succeeds without the sandbox, so the test proves the sandbox is what stops it.

## Done when

- Both CI jobs run the suite on every pull request, and every route fails under the sandbox and succeeds in the control.

## Related

- #141"}

 {"key":"spike","title":"Spike: test the sandbox assumptions on a Mac before RFC-0011","labels":["security","testing","P1"],"body":"## Why

The sandbox plan in #141 rests on three assumptions no one has tested. RFC-0011 and the setup skill should be written against what is true, not what is assumed.

## What to do

- [ ] With a throwaway Claude Code profile on macOS, turn on `sandbox.enabled`, `failIfUnavailable` and `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`.

- [ ] **Hooks.** Check that the plugin's hooks run outside the sandbox: from a hook, read a file that the sandbox denies to Bash.
- [ ] **MCP server.** Check that a plugin-bundled MCP server runs outside the sandbox, with the user's normal gh login, and that a PreToolUse hook matches its tool names.
- [ ] **Edit deny rules.** Check whether `Edit` deny rules for the layer's records also stop sandboxed Bash from writing them, and whether a symbolic link inside the project to a denied path is denied too.
- [ ] Record each result, with the exact settings and commands used, as a comment on #141.

## Done when

- Each assumption has a recorded yes or no, and #141's design is adjusted where an answer is no.

## Related

 {"key":"rfc","title":"RFC-0011: a declared OS boundary as the condition for relaxing a shell call","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

Standard 1.2.0 §5.18.3 lets a layer classify a call from its arguments and relax it below the tool's worst case. For a shell, that classification reads text, which cannot be made sound (#141). Standard 1.2.0 is still a Candidate, so this can be fixed before it is released.

## What to do

- [ ] Write `spec/RFC-0011-*.md` with the sections `spec/GOVERNANCE.md` requires (motivation, alternatives, backward compatibility, conformance tests), marked as amending Standard 1.2.0.
- [ ] §10.4: a conformance statement names, for each shell-like tool, the operating-system boundary its calls run under, or "none".
- [ ] §5.18.3: a classifier may relax a call of such a tool below the tool's worst case only when a boundary is declared. A layer without one stays conformant, with every call of the tool at its worst case.
- [ ] Define what a boundary must hold for this purpose: writes limited to the scope, no write to the layer's records, a network allowlist, and the layer's own credentials out of reach.
- [ ] Update the statement schema (`tests/conformance/calls/schema/statement.schema.json`), both reference statements, `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` and the CHANGELOG.
- [ ] Use the spike's findings.

## Done when

- RFC-0011 is Accepted and Standard 1.2.0 carries the rule.
- `python tools/validate_rfcs.py` passes, and both statements declare their boundary.

## Related

- #141, #137 (the release waits for this)"},
 {"key":"setup","title":"Add a setup skill that writes the sandbox settings","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

A plugin cannot change a user's settings on its own. Without the sandbox settings, every Bash call stays gated under RFC-0011, so users need a guided way to turn the sandbox on.

## What to do

- [ ] Add a skill (`/grounded-setup`) that shows the settings it will write as a diff, asks, then writes them to user scope (`~/.claude/settings.json`):
  - `sandbox.enabled: true`, `failIfUnavailable: true`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, and no `excludedCommands`;
  - `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` (see the network allowlist sub-issue);
  - Edit and Read deny rules for the layer's records (see the deny-rules sub-issue);
  - credential deny entries for the audit key file and for the usual token files and variables: `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`, `~/.git-credentials`, `~/.ssh`, `GH_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
- [ ] Leave every other setting alone, and keep the skill safe to run again.
- [ ] On a platform with no sandbox (native Windows), say so and write nothing.
- [ ] Document it in `hooks/README.md` and the README.

## Done when

- On a fresh macOS and Linux profile, running the skill and accepting gives settings under which the relax rule applies and the boundary tests pass.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"relax","title":"Relax read-only Bash only under a verified strict sandbox (plugin hook)","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

Under RFC-0011, the pre-tool-use hook may let a read-only Bash command skip the checkpoint and approval only when an operating-system boundary holds.

## What to do

- [ ] In `hooks/pretooluse_require_checkpoint.sh`, read the effective `sandbox` settings from user and managed settings only, never from the project's, which a repository controls.
- [ ] Relax read-only Bash only when `enabled`, `failIfUnavailable` and `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` all hold. Otherwise classify every Bash call as a gated `mutate`.
- [ ] Treat a Bash call that sets `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` as a gated `mutate`.
- [ ] Say in the refusal text how to enable the sandbox (the setup skill).
- [ ] Tests: a sandbox off, missing, or partly configured in each scope; project settings that try to claim a sandbox.

## Done when

- With the strict sandbox, read-only commands pass as today. Without it, every Bash call needs a checkpoint and approval. Project settings cannot change which applies.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"deny","title":"Protect the layer's records with deny rules, not the records guard","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

The records guard decides from command text whether a call writes the layer's records (`.claude/checkpoint.ok`, `.claude/checkpoints/`, `.claude/audit.log` and its head, `<git dir>/acs/`). ## What to do

- [ ] Define Edit and Read deny rules for those paths, as the setup skill writes them.

- [ ] Document the records guard as an advisory early refusal (`hooks/README.md`, SECURITY.md §5.5).
- [ ] Boundary tests: write each record from Bash and from Edit or Write, through several spellings and a link, and expect each attempt to fail.

## Done when

- Under the setup skill's settings, no Bash command or file tool writes a record, whatever its spelling.

## Related

- #141, #143"},
 {"key":"network","title":"Fill the sandbox's network allowlist from the domain profile","labels":["enhancement","security","P2"],"body":"## Why

## What to do

- [ ] Document the send hook as advisory.
- [ ] Boundary tests: reach an unlisted host, a private address and the cloud metadata address from Bash, through several spellings, and expect each to fail.

## Done when

- Under the setup skill's settings, Bash reaches only the listed hosts.

## Related

- #141"},
 {"key":"key","title":"Keep the audit log's HMAC key in a file out of the agent's reach","labels":["enhancement","security","P1"],"body":"## Why

The log hook signs the audit log with `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY`. When that is unset, it derives the key from the hostname, which any process can recompute. The agent's own commands can also read the variable, so a cut log can be signed again.

- [ ] Keep `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` working where it is set, for compatibility, and say in the docs that the file is preferred.
- [ ] Update `tools/verify_audit_log.py`, SECURITY.md, `hooks/README.md` and the CHANGELOG (an upgrade note).
- [ ] Boundary test: read the key from Bash and from Read, and expect both to fail.

## Done when

- Under the setup skill's settings, nothing the agent runs can read the key, and no key is derived from the hostname.

## Related

content.text: Creating the ten sub-issues and attaching each to #141:

input.command:
REDACTED; python3 - $S <<'EOF' > $S/created.tsv
import json,subprocess,sys
S=sys.argv[1]
R="synaptiai/agent-capability-standard"
for it in json.load(open(f"{S}/subissues.json")):
    args=["gh","issue","create","--repo",R,"--title",it["title"],"--body",it["body"]]
    for l in it["labels"]: args+=["--label",l]
    url=subprocess.run(args,capture_output=True,text=True,check=True).stdout.strip()
    num=url.rsplit("/",1)[1]
    iid=subprocess.run(["gh","api",f"repos/{R}/issues/{num}","--jq",".id"],capture_output=True,text=True,check=True).stdout.strip()
    r=subprocess.run(["gh","api","-X","POST",f"repos/{R}/issues/141/sub_issues","-F",f"sub_issue_id={iid}"],capture_output=True,text=True)
    print(f"{it['key']}\t{num}\t{'attached' if r.returncode==0 else 'ATTACH FAILED '+r.stderr.strip()[:80]}")
EOF

1. **The agent's shell.** On macOS, Claude Code runs the agent's commands in the user's login shell, zsh by default, while the hooks read commands as bash 5 does. zsh's code-running forms are gated because the hooks can't read them, and the gap is recorded in SECURITY.md 5.5 (PR #176).
2. **What a sandbox does not solve.** A sandbox under the agent's commands (#141) closes most text-reading gaps, but three remain for this issue:
   - **Trust handoff:** a file the agent writes that another tool later runs (git hooks, editor tasks, CI configuration).
   - **Fail-open defaults:** a sandbox that runs commands unsandboxed when it can't start, unless failIfUnavailable is set.
   - **Authorised destruction:** a force push or a deploy with a valid credential. #185 moves remote writes to typed tools for this reason." >/dev/null && echo 144; gh issue close 146 --repo $R --reason "not planned" --comment "Closed as not planned: under the sandbox epic (#141), the shell-text readers are frozen as advisory and get no new cases. The readers keep the union of the bash 5.2 and 5.3 readings, which fails closed. On macOS, bash 3.2 reads some braces differently again, and the agent's shell is zsh; both gaps are recorded in SECURITY.md 5.5 (PR #176)." >/dev/null && echo 146-closed

content.text:
So far, the PR's CI is still running, I've changed the issue tracker on GitHub, and nothing is merged. Here's where things stand:

- **#134 (macOS) is fixed in PR #176.** On a stock Mac the hook tests went from 1,765 failures to none. The fixes:
  - **Skill hooks blocking everything.** Three skill hooks couldn't be parsed by bash 3.2, so they blocked every command.
  - **A missed credential.** BSD grep silently skipped the rule that finds `curl -u user:password` credentials.
  - **Link handling.** One link case let a new file be written into the audit records' directory, and another followed the wrong file.

  A new CI job runs every test on macOS, with both the system bash 3.2 and Homebrew's bash.
- **Tests I changed rather than fixed, which you should know about:**
  - **Timing tests.** These now check that time grows linearly with the input on macOS, instead of using the Linux limits. The scan really is about ten times slower there. A Write of about 3.5 MB runs past the 30-second hook limit and gets blocked.
  - **Bash behaviour tests.** Six tests that probe what bash itself does skip on bash 3.2.
  - **The `SHELLOPTS=noexec` test.** It skips where `/bin/sh` is bash. That's a gap SECURITY.md already documents: Claude Code starts the hook through that shell, so the setting stops it before any hook code runs.

  The gaps are recorded in the docs, not hidden.
- **Something we found along the way.** On this Mac, Claude Code runs the agent's commands in zsh, while the hooks read them as bash. That's more evidence for the sandbox direction. A probe showed zsh's code-running forms are still blocked, because the hooks can't read them.
- **One test failure is an artefact of my session.** The flow plugin's git shim on my `PATH` broke one test locally. It passes without the shim, so I left that test alone.
- **The sandbox plan is now on GitHub.**
  - #141 is the epic, with ten sub-issues (#177–#186).
  - #146 is closed as not planned.
  - #142, #143, #144 and the tracking issue #133 have notes on how they change.
  - Our decisions are also saved in `REDACTED.md`.
- **Your Mac now has Homebrew bash 5.3**, first on `PATH`.
- **The handoff branch still isn't on main.** The handoff and its lesson are two commits on `claude/gallant-hypatia-wbucn3` with no pull request.

I did this work by hand rather than through `/flow:start`, and I didn't run a PVC (perspective review) for the PR; its description says why. When CI finishes I'll report the result and move on to the spike (#177). That's the next step in the order you agreed: it checks on this Mac whether a sandboxed command can read your gh and git tokens from the keychain.
